title: Is Saudi Arabia’s debt strategy sustainable?
gist: Saudi Arabia financed its entire H1 2026 deficit through debt rather than reserves as financing costs jumped 41% y/y, but geo-economic analyst Rachel Ziemba argues the Kingdom remains solvent -- built for this exact two-front war scenario -- even as ratings agencies watch for medium-term stress in external accounts, FDI shortfalls, and Red Sea logistics costs.

themes.theme: H1 2026 deficit financed entirely by borrowing

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia financed its entire first-half 2026 budget deficit of SAR 160 billion through borrowing, drawing nothing from government reserves.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Signals a deliberate choice to preserve reserve buffers even as debt servicing costs climb — watch Saudi issuance calendar and spread trends.
insights.locator: The entire first-half deficit of SAR 160 bn

insights.claim: Saudi public debt rose to SAR 1.685 trillion by end-June 2026, up from SAR 1.519 trillion at the start of the year, while financing expenses (interest cost) rose 41% year-on-year in the second quarter alone.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A 41% jump in interest costs in one quarter is a fast-rising fiscal drag investors should track against oil price offsets.
insights.locator: Public debt climbed to SAR 1.685 tn

insights.claim: Rachel Ziemba says Saudi Arabia's growing reliance on debt predates the current war and reflects the underlying costs of economic diversification and asset-leveraging strategy, not just wartime spending.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The debt build-up is structural, not a temporary war effect — deleveraging is unlikely even after a ceasefire.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia’s increasing reliance on debt extends well before the war, reflecting the extensive costs of diversification and desire to leverage assets to meet economic goals
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia’s increasing reliance on debt extends

insights.claim: Ziemba attributes the widening deficit less to lower oil revenue (partly offset by higher prices) and more to a rise in spending needs since the conflict began.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Spending-side pressure, not just a revenue shortfall, is the deficit driver — fiscal consolidation would require cutting outlays, not just an oil price rally.
insights.quote: With the conflict, the oil revenue piece is down but partly offset by higher prices
insights.locator: With the conflict, the oil revenue piece

themes.theme: Rising rate exposure via US Treasury spreads

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia is better placed to absorb the fiscal hit from the conflict than regional peers such as Iraq or Bahrain, per Ziemba.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Relative fiscal resilience argues for differentiating Saudi sovereign risk from weaker Gulf/regional peers.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia is still better placed to absorb

insights.claim: Rising US Treasury yields directly raise Saudi Arabia's own borrowing spreads, exposing the Kingdom to the same global rate cycle as every other sovereign borrower.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Saudi financing costs are a levered play on US rates — a higher-for-longer Fed path compounds the Kingdom's already-rising interest bill.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia faces challenges as US Treasury rates, and thus Saudi spreads, go up.
insights.locator: Saudi Arabia faces challenges as US Treasury

themes.theme: Ratings agencies still see solvency despite stress

insights.claim: Fitch affirmed Saudi Arabia's A+ sovereign rating on 12 July 2026, citing strong fiscal buffers and external finances even amid regional conflict and trade disruption, while flagging oil dependence and governance as constraints.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Rating affirmation despite war conditions supports continued market access at reasonable spreads for now.
insights.locator: Fitch affirmed the Kingdom’s A+ rating on 12 July

insights.claim: Moody's affirmed Saudi Arabia's Aa3 rating in May 2026.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A second major agency holding its rating reinforces the market's current calm on Saudi credit risk.

insights.claim: Ratings agencies are distinguishing between countries that are fiscally stressed and those that are geopolitically stressed but solvent, and currently place Saudi Arabia in the solvent camp.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: This framework is the key lens for tracking a potential Saudi downgrade: watch for language shifting from 'solvent despite conflict' to 'fiscally stressed'.
insights.quote: Saudi Arabia faces a structural fiscal weakness, but a manageable one, and additional stresses from the conflict
insights.locator: Ratings agencies are drawing a line between

insights.claim: Investors have remained relatively upbeat on Saudi risk because higher oil prices are partly compensating for the fiscal strain, but Ziemba warns the larger effects of the war may only show up over the medium term.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Current investor calm may be underpricing medium-term risk — a gap between headline sentiment and structural exposure worth monitoring.
insights.quote: Investors have been relatively upbeat about Saudi risk given the higher oil prices that partly compensate, but the bigger effects may be medium-term in nature.
insights.locator: Investors are still showing up, for now

themes.theme: Reserves and PIF built for exactly this scenario

insights.claim: Ziemba says the ongoing two-front pressure -- Iranian strikes, Houthi attacks on shipping and oil infrastructure, and the prospect of a Yemen ground campaign -- is precisely the scenario Saudi Arabia built its reserve buffer for.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The reserve buffer being used as originally intended is a bullish signal for near-term solvency, even as debt levels climb.
insights.quote: This is one of the reasons why Saudi Arabia saved, and why the PIF was already turning mostly domestic.

insights.claim: How long Saudi Arabia's debt-financing strategy can hold depends on whether it can keep diverting oil and other supplies through new channels despite the conflict.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Watch Saudi export routing and channel diversification data as a leading indicator of fiscal sustainability.
insights.quote: whether Saudi Arabia is able to continue diverting supplies through new channels.

insights.claim: Attracting foreign direct investment into Saudi Arabia's key diversification projects remains difficult, meaning the Saudi government itself will likely keep functioning as the main investor behind its own diversification agenda.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Weak FDI means Vision 2030-style projects stay reliant on state and PIF balance sheets rather than private capital -- a structural drag on the debt trajectory.
insights.quote: Attracting FDI into key projects remains difficult
insights.locator: She flags a structural issue underneath the calm

themes.theme: War costs hidden outside the budget line

insights.claim: Ziemba argues the full cost structure of the war -- including war-risk insurance premiums and the cost of rerouting shipments around Red Sea chokepoints -- must be weighed separately from the headline budget deficit figure.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Headline deficit numbers understate the true fiscal burden of the conflict; investors should look for shipping and insurance cost data as a supplement to budget releases.
insights.quote: the “full cost structure” of the war has to be weighed separately from the budget line, including war-risk premiums and the cost of rerouting shipments around Red Sea chokepoints.
insights.locator: The external accounts are the part that doesn’t show up

insights.claim: Ziemba expects the war to reinforce Saudi Arabia's interest in import substitution, including construction inputs, which will support the domestic mining sector.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A concrete sector call: war-driven import substitution is a tailwind for Saudi mining and domestic materials plays.
insights.quote: This will support the mining sector.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia is expected to seek greater cargo throughput and transshipment business from other countries that lack their own port infrastructure, as the war reshapes Red Sea and Gulf logistics.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Saudi ports could gain regional transshipment share as a byproduct of Red Sea disruption -- a logistics-sector angle on the conflict.
insights.quote: looking to attract cargo throughput from other countries

insights.claim: Ratings agencies will next be watching demand shifts and the return on recent Saudi government investments, a test that has not yet arrived.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The next credit inflection point is not the current deficit print but whether state-led investment projects start generating returns.
